issues.legal_issue: A trust that holds government land on the government’s behalf and constructs premises with government funds does not acquire ownership merely because it manages the property, may make limited dealings with it, or the property is described as vesting in it.
material_facts: The land on which the market was built belonged to the government before it was placed at the Trust’s disposal.
The agreement required the Trust to hold and manage the land on the government’s behalf and to keep separate accounts for the property.

The market was constructed with funds advanced by the government, and income from the property was to be applied to specified expenses and obligations, with any surplus placed at the government’s disposal.
The Trust’s power to sell or lease the property was subject to conditions and government or Chief Commissioner approval in specified circumstances.

The statute and agreement contained no express conveyance of title to the Trust; the government could terminate the arrangement, and the relevant transfer provision required reimbursement of costs rather than payment of the property’s market value.
issues.conclusion: The Trust was a statutory agent of the government, and both the market and the land on which it stood remained government property.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 54A(1) and (2) of the U.P. Town Improvement Act, as extended to Delhi, placing property at a Trust’s disposal does not itself transfer title; the agreement and statutory context determine the nature of the Trust’s interest. The word “vest” has no fixed meaning and may refer to possession, a limited interest, or title depending on context: Richardson v. Robertson; Hinde v. Charlton; Coverdale v. Charlton; In re Brown (a lunatic); and Finchley Electric Light Company v. Finchley Urban District Council. The Court also relied on Bhatia Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. D.C. Patel in considering the ownership of a structure erected on another’s land under an agreement.

rule.if: property_ownership_dispute and government_owned_underlying_land and trust_holds_property_for_government and government_financed_construction and trust_disposal_powers_are_restricted

predicates.property_ownership_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to determine who owns premises held or managed by a public trust.
predicates.government_owned_underlying_land: The government owned the land before it was made available to the trust.
predicates.trust_holds_property_for_government: The trust holds and manages the property on the government’s behalf under an arrangement that preserves government control over its use or income.
predicates.government_financed_construction: The government supplied the funds used to construct the premises.
predicates.trust_disposal_powers_are_restricted: The trust can sell or lease the property only subject to material conditions or government approval.

issues.definition: When an ownership dispute concerns government land held for the government by a trust, and the government funded construction while restricting the trust’s disposal powers, the premises remain government-owned.

issues.legal_issue: Premises owned by the government and managed by its statutory agent are outside the protection of the rent-control law, so a tenant whose lease has ended may be ejected.
material_facts: The market and its underlying land remained government property, while the Trust managed the property as the government’s statutory agent.
The tenant’s lease had a stated term and required the tenant to vacate and deliver possession when the lease expired or was determined.
The tenant sought protection under the rent-control law and an injunction against eviction after the lease term ended.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control law did not apply to the premises, and the tenant was liable to ejectment upon termination of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(a) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 excludes government premises from the Act. Because the premises remained government property and the Trust acted as the government’s statutory agent, the Act’s operative provisions did not protect the tenant after the lease ended. Section 54A of the U.P. Town Improvement Act, as extended to Delhi, and the agreement supported the conclusion that the property remained government property.

predicates.rent_control_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a tenant’s claim to protection from eviction under a rent-control regime.
predicates.premises_are_government_owned: The premises are owned by the government, although another body may manage or lease them.
predicates.lease_term_has_ended: The tenant’s lease has expired or has otherwise been terminated.

issues.definition: In a rent-control proceeding, if the premises are government-owned and the lease has ended, rent-control protection is unavailable and ejectment is permitted.
